notes.body:
The teacher's examples — hunger, anger, thirst — use the body's inability to sustain intensity as the reason for temporariness. The same holds for a divine attribute, but through a different mechanism. **The limit is not in Allah; it is in creation.** The فعلان pattern describes the quality as it lands on, and is experienced by, whoever receives it — not what the source can sustain.

Think of the sun. It neither tires of shining nor is diminished by being felt. But you cannot stare into it without going blind. Allah's رحمة, in its most intense mode, is not constrained by any limit in Him — but creation can only absorb so much before it overwhelms the faculties that allow us to recognize and benefit from it.

The etymology of رحمن reveals this most beautifully. The root ر-ح-م gives us رحم — the womb — the most total and unconditional care we know. **It provides everything: warmth, nourishment, protection, without asking anything in return.** And yet the child must leave — not because the womb's love ended, but because continued dwelling would prevent the very growth the love intended. The intensity withdraws for the sake of the one being loved.

This is precisely why الرحمن and الرحیم always appear together:

- الرحمن: extreme, immediate, and temporary — like the womb's total immersion
- الرحیم: permanent and enduring — the mother's love after the child is born

Neither alone is sufficient. One gives the overwhelming present burst; the other gives the quiet guarantee that holds across time. Together, they are **the only honest way to describe love that is both fully present and always there.**

Ibn Abbas said simply: Allah is الرحمن in this life and الرحیم in the next. The intense mercy pours on everyone now — believer and disbeliever alike, as rain falls on all. That distinction is not about Allah's capacity. It is about the conditions under which creation receives.

notes.quote: All word that match this pattern will always possess these 3 characteristics. They will be extreme; they will be immediate; and they will be temporary.
etymology: رحمن: from root ر-ح-م (رحم). رحم means the womb — the origin and enclosure of new life. Real Quranic derivatives: رَّحِيم, رَحْمَة, رَّحْمَٰن. The root carries a tenderness so total it holds the beloved entirely within itself. رحمن adds the فعلان pattern: extreme in force, immediate in action, and — like the womb's own care — temporary in its most intense form.

رحیم: same root ر-ح-م, shaped by the فعيل pattern (as in كريم, حكيم, جميل). This pattern marks a settled, permanent disposition — a quality that defines the one who carries it, not merely an action happening right now. رحيم is the love that outlasts every moment: abiding, steady, and structurally guaranteed.

notes.body:
The apparent contradiction dissolves once we understand what الرحمن is saying at the grammatical level. Arabic has a phonetic pattern — the آن form — that always carries three qualities together: extreme in degree, immediate in time, and temporary by nature. غضبان means furiously angry, right this moment, but no one sustains that fury forever. جوعان means ravenously hungry, right now, but hunger ends. الرحمن works the same way: overwhelming, immediate, and not designed to last indefinitely.

**The universality of الرحمن is real** — it falls on everyone without discrimination, the way rain falls from the sky. The believer drinks that rain and the denier drinks it equally. We are told:

رَحْمَتِی وَسِعَتْ عَلَیٰ کُلِّ شَیْءٍ
My mercy encompasses all things.
Al-A'raf 7:156

None of that universality contradicts the temporary character baked into the word. The door is open to everyone during this life; the invitation never expires here. Temporary does not mean stingy — it means the intense, overwhelming surge of mercy belongs to this world specifically.

When someone asked Ibn Abbas about the difference between الرحمن and الرحیم, he answered with quiet precision: in this life, Allah is الرحمن for everyone; in the next life, he is الرحیم for the believers. الرحیم follows the یم pattern — the same pattern as كريم and حكيم — which marks something permanent and deeply characteristic, not immediate but lasting. When the universal surge of الرحمن concludes at the end of this world, الرحیم continues — but for those who chose to walk through the open door while the light was on.

A door is wide open to everyone during the day. The invitation falls equally on anyone standing outside. But it is still a daytime door — when day ends, it closes. Together they leave no gap: **the pair covers both this life and the next**, the overwhelming and the enduring, the universal and the particular.

notes.quote: the love and care of Allah will go away for disbelievers on the day of judgment
etymology: رحمن: from root ر-ح-م, whose core meaning is warmth and tenderness — directly connected to رَحِم (the womb), the most intimate shelter of care that exists. The آن suffix drives the meaning to its extreme: intense, immediate, and temporary, just as غضبان means fury at its peak right now, impossible to sustain forever. Derivatives: رَحْمَة, رَحِمَ.

رحيم: same root ر-ح-م, but the يم suffix — shared with كَرِيم (generous) and حَكِيم (wise) — marks a quality that is settled and enduring rather than a surge. Where رحمن names an overwhelming act of mercy happening now, رحيم names a permanent identity: one for whom mercy is simply who they are, reliably and without condition.
